report:
## Conclusion: The claim is well-supported by high-quality evidence.

**Key evidence supporting the claim:**

The landmark **Devinsky et al. (2017) NEJM trial** — a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 120 children and young adults with Dravet syndrome — found that add-on cannabidiol (CBD) at 20 mg/kg/day produced a **median 38.9% reduction** in convulsive seizure frequency versus **13.3% with placebo** (P=0.01). 5% of CBD-treated patients became seizure-free vs. 0% on placebo. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618))

A subsequent **dose-ranging RCT** (Devinsky et al., 2020, JAMA Neurology) confirmed that both tested CBD doses significantly reduced convulsive seizures compared with placebo in treatment-resistant Dravet syndrome. ([JAMA Neurology](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamaneurology/fullarticle/2762458))

A **systematic review and meta-analysis** (Lattanzi et al., 2020, CNS Drugs) pooled multiple RCTs and confirmed CBD's efficacy as adjunctive therapy for Dravet syndrome seizures. ([Springer/CNS Drugs](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s40263-020-00708-6))

**Limitations and counterpoints:**

- **Adverse events** were significantly more common with CBD, including somnolence, diarrhea, vomiting, fatigue, pyrexia, and elevated liver enzymes. More patients withdrew from the CBD group. ([NEJM](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1611618))
- CBD did **not** significantly reduce nonconvulsive seizures, and only a small minority achieved seizure freedom. ([PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5716495/))
- Trials were relatively short (14 weeks), and long-term extension data, while encouraging, came from open-label designs. ([Wiley/Epilepsia](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1111/epi.14628))
- CBD interacts with other antiepileptic drugs (notably clobazam), raising questions about how much of its effect is independent. ([NeurologyLive](https://www.neurologylive.com/view/clearing-up-confusion-about-cannabidiol-dravet-syndrome))

**Bottom line:** Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses consistently demonstrate that add-on pharmaceutical-grade CBD significantly reduces convulsive seizure frequency in children with Dravet syndrome. The claim is true, though benefits are modest, not all patients respond, and adverse effects and drug interactions are meaningful considerations.
